column3: It repeats the hand's protected insertion, white emergence without harm, and its role as a proof before Pharaoh.
It closely restates the hand entering its covering and emerging white without harm among Moses' signs.
Its broken promise to depart with an expelled group does not clarify Moses' bodily sign.
The lowered wing offers a secondary image for the focus ayah's wing or side, though in a distinct ethical setting.
The immediate continuation identifies the hand transformation as one of the great signs shown to Moses.
Waiting for someone to come out supplies only a distant contrast to the controlled emergence of Moses' hand.
It shows the same visible white hand before onlookers, confirming the public manifestation of the sign.
Divine choosing, forgiveness, and guidance provide only broad background within the same surah.
The proposed payment for a barrier is unrelated to the hand sign.
It repeats the white hand's appearance to observers in the Moses narrative.
Moses' following prayer begins the mission for which the displayed signs are given.

Being brought forth for humanity is a remote communal use of emergence.
A tree emerging from Hell does not illuminate the hand sign.
The later reward for faithful deeds is only broad same-surah context.
God's bringing living and dead from each other offers a general divine-power parallel.

Moses' request for Aaron continues the mission preparation following the signs.
Adam and his spouse being expelled from the garden concerns a different kind of departure.
The refusal to extend a hand for killing is a distant ethical contrast to the commanded hand sign.
The reward of the purified adds little to the specific miracle.
The command expelling Iblis does not clarify Moses' hand emerging from concealment.
God's reminder of an earlier favor broadens the divine preparation of Moses that includes the signs.
The staff swallowing deception is the companion miracle in Moses' public sign encounter.
Water emerging from stones is not a useful parallel to the transformed hand.
God's bringing people forth again displays divine power of emergence within the same surah, but in a distinct setting.

Moses' fearful departure from the city is a separate episode, with only a broad Moses connection.
Difficulty for disbelievers has no material link to the sign.
Israel's deliverance and provision are later Moses-narrative context rather than an explanation of the hand sign.
Turning one's face after departing gives only a remote movement parallel.
Mockery at a sign only broadly reflects the reception of miraculous signs.
Moses asks that Aaron strengthen him, continuing the immediate mission preparation.
The inability to leave the Fire does not clarify the sign.
A false word coming from mouths is only a distant contrast to a visible divine sign.
The question about what is in Moses' right hand begins the immediate sequence of signs leading to the focus ayah.
Grain brought from revived earth does not clarify the hand miracle.
The legal provision concerning a widow's residence is unrelated.
The question about the great news offers only a broad interrogative/sign context.
Direction after departure is unrelated to the transformed hand.
Turning away from every divine sign helps frame the public challenge posed by Moses' signs.
Moses' request to share his task with Aaron continues the adjacent mission context.
Turning toward peace is a figurative use of the same wing-root and not the bodily sign.
Its statement that people turn away from divine signs provides a general reception context.
The command to lead God's servants by night continues the later Moses narrative and divine protection.
Resurrection imagery through revived land does not clarify the hand sign.
The she-camel as a sign, protected from harm, gives only a broad sign-and-harm parallel.
A possible sign from heaven does not explain Moses' specific hand sign.

Moses' purpose of abundant glorification continues the immediate explanation of his mission.
The contrast between human payment and God's provision is unrelated.

The earth bringing out its burdens is a distant emergence image.

Jesus' sign from his Lord offers a general prophetic-sign parallel, not the hand miracle.

The guarding recorders do not illuminate the sign.

Moses' staff becomes a moving serpent immediately before the hand sign, establishing the paired sequence of miracles.
The command to seize the transformed staff without fear clarifies the controlled restoration and divine command surrounding the next sign.
The command to go to Pharaoh identifies the mission toward which the hand sign is directed.
God's granting of Moses' requests confirms the mission preparation that follows the displayed signs.
The later statement that Pharaoh was shown all the signs explicitly frames the hand transformation within their cumulative public presentation.
Pharaoh's demand that Moses bring a sign directly introduces the paired staff and white-hand displays that follow.
Moses casts his staff before the white-hand sign, supplying the first half of the paired proof shown to Pharaoh's assembly.
The command to cast the staff begins the same Moses sign sequence that proceeds to the hand entering its covering.
The staff's transformation and Moses' fearful retreat directly precede the command to insert his hand and the two proofs.
Its reference to the nine clear signs given to Moses places the hand miracle within the wider sign corpus shown to Pharaoh.
